html:
Mississippian towns were farming centres with large earthen platform mounds that spread across the Mississippi valley and the American Southeast from about 1000 to the 1500s. The greatest of them was Cahokia, near modern St Louis.

Mississippian life rested on maize, grown together with older native crops of the Eastern Agricultural Complex. Towns had a plaza with flat-topped mounds, where chiefs' houses and temples stood. Chiefs ruled groups of towns, and their power seems to have rested on religion, feasting and control of trade in copper, shell and stone.

Cahokia grew fast after about 1050. At its peak around 1100 it may have held 10,000 to 20,000 people, about as many as London at the time. Its centre was Monks Mound, the largest earthwork in the Americas, covering about 6 hectares at its base. Around it lay a great plaza, more than a hundred other mounds, and circles of wooden posts used to track the sun. Some burials there include many people killed in ritual.

Cahokia was largely empty by about 1350, perhaps from floods, drought, overuse of wood and political strife. Other Mississippian chiefdoms carried on in the South. In 1539 to 1543 the Spanish expedition of Hernando de Soto met some of them. The diseases and wars that followed broke them apart, and their peoples regrouped as nations such as the Creek, Choctaw and Chickasaw. It was the same era as Chaco Canyon in the Southwest.
sum: Mississippian towns were farming centres with large earthen platform mounds that spread across the Mississippi valley and the American Southeast from about 1000 to the 1500s. The greatest of them was Cahokia, near modern St Louis.
